DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The pilot data are useful and the cost table adds up, but the study's main conclusions don't follow from its own figures. Flats behaved very differently from houses. The tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot data. Brookfield can only take part of the projected tonnage. Once these are corrected, the claim that the service is "fully funded" no longer holds.

## 1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses

| Housing type | Participation | Yield per participating household |
|---|---|---|
| Houses | **66%** | 1.9 kg |
| Flats | **21%** | 1.4 kg |

Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types," and the recommendation relies on that. Your summary says participation "held up across houses and flats." **Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses**, and those that did took part produced less per household.

This is the most important finding in the pilot, and it points the other way from the recommendation. Flats are 20% of the district, about 10,400 households, and are likely to need a different approach, such as communal bins, collection points or targeted engagement. A 23-litre outdoor caddy for each flat may not suit them at all. The roll-out plan and budget should allow for this.

## 2. The projection uses a 64% participation rate that isn't in the data

The pilot's overall participation was **57%** (2,280 ÷ 4,000). Section 3 applies **64%**, which matches no figure in Table 1. The district has the same mix as the pilot (20% flats), so the pilot rates by housing type carry over directly:

| | Households | Participation | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | about 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | about 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | **57%** | **about 2,870** |

The study projects **3,290 tonnes**, an overstatement of about **420 tonnes (15%)**. On the corrected figure, the disposal saving falls from £243,000 to about **£213,000**.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Brookfield has offered **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Even the corrected projection is about **2,870 tonnes**, leaving roughly **1,070 tonnes a year** with no costed destination. The options are:

- **The 46-mile plant.** Its gate fee and the extra haulage costs (vehicle time, fuel, crew hours) are not included.
- **Incineration.** That gives no saving on that tonnage and defeats the purpose of separate collection.

If only 1,800 tonnes are diverted at the £74 saving, the saving is about **£133,000**, not £243,000. Your summary's description of treatment as "local" is only true for about 60% of the tonnage.

## 4. The funding claim doesn't hold

The cost lines check out: £990,000 of vehicles over 7 years = £141,400, crews = £408,000, and the total is £733,400. But the net cost depends on the saving:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520,000 allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all to Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, all to Brookfield | about £213,000 | about £521,000 | **about £1,000 short** |
| Brookfield cap of 1,800 t, rest incinerated | about £133,000 | about £600,000 | **about £80,000 short** |

The excess could instead go to the 46-mile plant, which saves something but adds haulage. Either way, the cost falls between the last two rows and isn't included.

The **£520,000 is also provisional**, since the Government has only "indicated" funding. The study should show what happens if the final allocation is lower.

## 5. Costs that are missing or unclear

Your summary describes the financial analysis as "complete." Several items are missing:

- **Capital funding for the vehicles.** The £990,000 must be paid around December 2026 to March 2027. Depreciation spreads the *charge*, but the study doesn't say where the upfront cash comes from, or whether borrowing costs apply.
- **A spare vehicle and crew cover** for breakdowns, sickness and leave. With six vehicles and six crews, there is no margin.
- **Supervision, back-office and the dedicated phone line and web page** mentioned in Section 6.
- **Any separate service for flats** (see point 1).
- **Haulage and gate fees for tonnage above Brookfield's cap** (see point 3).

## 6. Smaller points

- **Timetable:** Vehicles ordered in December and delivered in March, with crews trained the same month and caddies arriving the same month, leaves no slack before a 5 April start. Confirm the supplier's lead time in writing, and set out a fallback such as hired vehicles.
- **Satisfaction figure:** The 81% comes from "surveyed pilot households." Give the response rate, and say whether non-participants were included. Satisfied participants are more likely to respond.
- **Seasonality:** The pilot ran January to June. Summer conditions, with smells and flies, can reduce participation. That doesn't invalidate the results, but it's worth noting.
- **The combined yield figure** of 1.9 kg is really about 1.86 kg when weighted. That's fine as a rounding, but it shouldn't be shown as identical to the houses figure.

## 7. What holds up

- **A strong evidence base:** 4,000 households, weekly measurement, and results by housing type.
- **Low contamination** (under 2%) and falling missed-collection reports.
- **A clear and checkable cost table.** All the arithmetic is correct.
- **A sensible link** to existing collection days.

## Notes on the author's summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Participation held up across houses and flats" | No: 66% against 21% |
| "Consistent yields" | 1.9 kg against 1.4 kg |
| Projection based on how residents "actually behave" | It uses 64%, not the pilot's 57% |
| "Every cost line is shown" | Capital funding, contingency, the flats service and overflow treatment are missing |
| Net cost "about £490,000, fully covered" | Only on the 64% figure with unlimited Brookfield capacity; otherwise short by up to about £80,000 |
| "Treatment is local" | For 1,800 tonnes; the rest isn't arranged |

## Recommended changes before Cabinet

1. **Correct the projection** to the pilot's rates by housing type (about 2,870 t).
2. **Rewrite the flats finding**, and set out and cost a separate approach for flats.
3. **Cost the tonnage above Brookfield's cap**, using the 46-mile plant's fee and haulage, or explain how it will be handled.
4. **Restate the net cost against the allocation**, with a sensitivity case for a lower final settlement.
5. **Add the capital funding route** for the vehicles, plus contingency and supervision costs.
6. **Confirm the vehicle lead time**, and include a fallback.

The case for going ahead is sound. The service is a legal requirement and the pilot is broadly positive. However, Cabinet should be told that it may need a top-up of up to about £80,000 a year and a separate plan for flats, not that it is "fully funded" and uniform.
